title: View From the Right
statement:
You get the root of a binary tree. Imagine standing to its right and looking at it level by level: on each level you see only the rightmost node of that level, whichever branch it belongs to.

Return the values you see, from the top level to the bottom. An empty tree gives an empty list.

Trees are written in level order with null for a missing child.

examples.why: The right branch stops at 14. Below that, the left branch is all you can see: 8 is the rightmost node on level 2 and 7 the only one on level 3. Following right children alone gives just [10, 14].
7 is a left child, but nothing on its level is further right, so it is visible.

constraints: The tree is at most 500 levels deep
hints: "The rightmost node of each level": which traversal already hands you the tree one level at a time?
With a level-by-level BFS, the answer for each level is simply the last node you take out of the queue in that round.
Or go depth-first, visiting the right child before the left and carrying the depth. The first node you reach at each new depth is the one seen from the right.

explain.intuition:
The tempting answer is to walk down the right children from the root. That fails as soon as the right branch is shorter than the left: from the right side you then see the left branch sticking out below it. What you actually see is the last node of each level, and levels are what BFS gives you. Run the row-by-row traversal and keep only the last value of every row.

A depth-first version works too. Visit the right child before the left one and carry the depth. The first time you reach a new depth, the node you are on is the rightmost one at that depth, since everything further right was visited before it. So record it when depth == answer.length and ignore later nodes at that depth. It is like a sticky table header: per level, only the first thing to arrive from the chosen direction stays visible.
steps: BFS: if the root is null, return []; otherwise put it in a queue.
Each round, note the queue's size: that many nodes make up the current level.
Take them out in order, queuing their children left then right. Remember the value of the last one.
Append that last value to the answer, and repeat until the queue is empty.
DFS alternative: walk(node, depth) records node.val when depth == answer.length, then calls right before left.
pitfalls: Following only right children. A deeper left branch is visible below a short right branch, like in the first example.
In the DFS version, visiting left before right. Then the first node at each depth is the leftmost one, which is the view from the other side.
In the BFS version, taking the first node of each round while queuing left before right. Either take the last one, or queue right children first.

complexity.space: O(w) for BFS, O(h) for DFS

solutions.title: BFS, keep the last node of each level
solutions.idea: Process the tree row by row. The last node taken out in each round is the rightmost one of that level.

solutions.title: DFS, right child first
solutions.idea: Visit right before left, carrying the depth. The first node reached at each depth is the one visible from the right.

followups: Return the view from the left. Which single change does each version need?
Return what you would see from directly above: the nodes visible per horizontal column. What do you need to track besides depth?
